metric.why: The ride-through chain is only as real as its weakest measurement. Batteries age silently, and fuel contracts measured in days assume deliveries that a regional emergency interrupts.
metric.metric: UPS battery health and generator runtime
metric.definition: Battery state of health and remaining runtime under current load, and on-site fuel measured in hours of generator operation at load.

reading.body:
Data centers track UPS battery health and generator runtime because uninterruptible power supply degradation and fuel supply gaps are invisible until they fail, and regional emergencies can break fuel delivery contracts measured in days.

The metric captures two different failure modes. Battery state of health decays with age and temperature cycles, reducing the window during which batteries can sustain load if grid power drops. Generator runtime depends on on-site fuel volume and consumption rate under actual load, which can shift as workloads change. Neither degrades in ways operators detect by watching power consumption alone. A battery that tests at 80% capacity still accepts a charge, but it cannot hold a charge as long as it did when new. A fuel tank half-full looks identical whether the generator burned through it in a week or will last two weeks at current draw.

For AI workloads specifically, this matters because peak compute demands are rising faster than facility design cycles can accommodate. A data center built to run at 70% nameplate power draws less on its backup systems than one running at 90%. If AI workloads push utilization up, runtime margins shrink silently. The metric does not measure grid reliability, fuel supply chain vulnerabilities, or the time required to bring additional generation online during an emergency. It measures only what is already on the site. It also does not track how often backup systems are actually tested or whether they have ever been run under real load conditions.
